analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage to $10.10 over three years and indexes it to inflation.
analysis.headline: A Senate majority of 54 voted to take up the minimum wage increase, but the vote fell short of the 60 needed, 54-42, and the bill never reached an up-or-down vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would raise the federal minimum wage in steps from $7.25 to $8.20, $9.15, and $10.10 an hour, then adjust it each year with inflation so it does not erode again. It would also raise the special lower wage for tipped workers, starting at $3.00 an hour and climbing until it equals 70% of the regular minimum. To offset employer costs, it extends tax rules letting businesses deduct the cost of equipment and certain property improvements up front, through 2016.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers paid at or near the federal minimum, including roughly part-time, food-service, and retail workers, would see a phased raise to $10.10 an hour with annual inflation adjustments. Tipped workers, whose base cash wage has been $2.13 an hour since 1991, would see it rise to $3.00 and then step up yearly toward 70% of the full minimum. Businesses that buy equipment, software, or make restaurant and retail property improvements also benefit from the extended expensing deduction.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal minimum wage in three steps to $10.10 an hour, then adjusts it annually by the Consumer Price Index so it never erodes again [S2] [S3].
Raises the cash wage for tipped employees from $2.13 to $3.00 an hour in the first year, with annual increases until it equals 70% of the regular minimum wage [S2] [S3].
Requires the Secretary of Labor to publish each upcoming wage adjustment at least 60 days in advance in the Federal Register and on the Labor Department website [S2] [S3].

Extends through tax years beginning before 2017 the increased $500,000 expensing allowance for business assets including software, and the treatment of leasehold, restaurant, and retail improvement property as depreciable business property [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers of low-wage workers bear higher payroll costs, concentrated in restaurants and food service, retail and wholesale trade. The federal treasury also bears the cost of the extended expensing deductions, which reduce tax revenue through 2016.

drawbacks.text: Employers of minimum-wage workers face phased increases in labor costs as the wage rises to $10.10, a cost borne most directly by restaurants, retail, and small businesses that employ many low-wage workers [S2] [S3].

Tipped workers would not reach parity with the full minimum wage for years; the tipped cash wage starts at just $3.00 an hour and only rises toward 70% of the regular minimum over successive years [S3].
The expensing extensions are a tax break for businesses that reduces federal revenue through tax years beginning before 2017, adding to the bill's cost [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — a raise to $10.10 for workers at the bottom, plus indexation that would end the cycle of the minimum wage losing value to inflation — is large and direct, and the tipped-wage phase-in is slower than full parity but a major increase from $2.13. The main costs are higher payroll expenses for low-wage employers and the revenue cost of the business expensing extensions, which were included to win support. Opponents' core objection, that mandated wage increases cost jobs, was the stated reason the Republican bloc blocked it.

outcome.mechanism: Senate Majority Leader Reid moved to proceed to the bill, and when Republicans objected, the Senate held a cloture vote on April 30, 2014 that needed 60 senators to let debate start; it failed 54-42, so the bill never got an up-or-down vote on its merits.

narrative.text: Senator Tom Harkin introduced the bill on April 8, 2014 with 39 cosponsors (38 Democrats and 1 independent), and it was placed on the Senate calendar within two days [S4] [S5].
Majority Leader Reid made repeated motions to proceed to consideration between April 10 and April 30, and presented a cloture motion on April 28 [S5].
On April 30, 2014, cloture on the motion to proceed failed 54-42, short of the 60 votes needed; 51 of 53 Democrats and both independents voted yes, while 41 of 45 Republicans voted no [S6].
Reid moved to reconsider the vote the same day, but no further action was taken before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who would have paid the higher wages — especially restaurants and the tipped-wage food service industry and low-wage retail — are better off, since their payroll costs stayed at $7.25 and $2.13. Businesses also kept the status quo on expensing rather than getting the extension, and no one received the raise.

for.name: Tom Harkin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Minimum Wage Fairness Act with 39 cosponsors and pressed for Senate consideration.

for.name: Harry Reid
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill and made repeated motions to proceed to consideration, then filed the cloture motion that forced the vote.

for.name: 39 Senate cosponsors
for.role: 38 Democrats and 1 independent cosponsoring the bill
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it a Democratic-plus-independent roster of support.

against.name: 41 of 45 Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: Voted no on the cloture motion to proceed, denying the 60 votes needed to bring the bill to the floor.

sides.party_line_note: The vote split almost entirely by party: 51 of 53 Democrats and both independents voted to proceed, while 41 of 45 Republicans voted no; only one Republican voted yes.

industries.note: Restaurants employ large numbers of minimum- and tipped-wage workers, so the bill would have raised both the regular and tipped wage floors, with the tipped wage climbing from $2.13 toward 70% of the minimum. The industry's interest in keeping wages flat runs against the workers whose pay the bill would raise.

Retail is a major employer at or near the minimum wage, so its labor costs would rise as the wage floor moved to $10.10; it also would have benefited from the extended property-improvement expensing, partially offsetting the cost.

industries.industry: Equipment and software sellers; businesses using expensing
industries.note: The bill extends the $500,000 Section 179 expensing allowance and favorable treatment of restaurant, retail, and leasehold improvement property through 2016, letting businesses deduct equipment and improvement costs immediately. This was the offset designed to ease the burden of the wage increase on employers.
